utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Groome, the Chamber was informed that you would like to address the Chamber and as we understood in relation to health and scheduling issues. Of course, if you want to raise any new matter, you're free to do so, but at this moment, nothing is pending before the Chamber. The scheduling issue is before the Appeals Chamber and we are in court here today. There is nothing at this moment to decide or to further consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are two matters. With respect to the -- I think the submission that the Chamber is referring to, I am down here in response to the Chamber's ruling yesterday evening that we would proceed without Mr. Mladic if absent clear medical indication. I agree that that is no longer -- he is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is here, so that's not anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would reserve that. I would ask the Chamber should we come to that moment again, that juncture again, I be given an opportunity to address the Chamber. With respect to the second matter, the second -- the next witness after Mr. Butler is Maria Karall. She is an employee of the OTP and her last day in the office is on Friday before she returns to her home country. The Prosecution is requesting that if Mr. Butler's examination is not concluded before Friday, that the Chamber intervene or interpose Ms. Karall's evidence so that she can complete it before she leaves the office. Her evidence is relatively short as the Chamber will see from the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any response by the Defence to that request? Mr. Lukic, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't receive English --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am supposed to be cross-examining the lady on Friday and we do not have a problem with hearing her testimony on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then -- if need be and if it could be arranged with Mr. Butler the Chamber does not oppose such a course of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity for the following: On the 6th of September of this year, the Defence has filed a motion for a 45-day extension of its deadline to file a response to the Prosecution's 33rd, 92 bis motion noting as support for its request the current heavy work load of the Defence. Having taken into consideration the Defence's current work load, as well as the relatively short and uncomplicated nature of the Prosecution's motion, the Chamber grants the Defence an additional two weeks in which to respond, setting the new deadline at the 23rd of September of 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony and you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you're ready I think we can begin. First of all, sir, are you proficient in the Serbian language so as to be able to speak, read and understand the same on your own?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the course of review of documents at the Office of the Prosecutor, did you reach conclusions based on a review of English translations of documents or did you use the original Serbian documents with the assistance of a translator?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the conclusions that I reached with respect to documents that were written in B/C/S, as the language as we called it, were done based off of the English-language translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you indicated, I think, in some of your reports that you reserved the right to supplement your reports and conclusions because there still existed a large body of documentation at the Office of the Prosecutor that had not been processed, and I presume translated, am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Particularly in 2003, we were just getting what were known as the tactical intercepts and then of course after I left we came into possession of the Drina Corps documents, so obviously as an analyst I hold open the possibility that new information may come available which may change me to, you know, change an opinion or a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to these documents, and written materials that had not yet been processed during your tenure at the Office of the Prosecutor or had not been translated, do you have an idea percentage-wise how much of the entire OTP collection relating to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina are we talking about? How much material did you not have access to to review for purposes of doing your work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess I don't understand the question. I mean, obviously as an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor I had access to all of the materials in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor with respect to documents. I could not hazard a guess as to what percentage the new tactical material and the new Drina Corps material made of the larger overall body of information. I don't think to this day anyone could even give you a count of the exact quantity of documents the Office of the Prosecutor thinks it holds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. Now, did you maintain a log of documents and materials that you either reviewed or consulted during the course of your work as an analyst and then also as an expert at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started to do that early on during my initial review of the documents and very rapidly it became clear that the sheer volume of documents if I were to continue that process I would spend all of my time logging documents as opposed to actually analysing them. What I have done and what I tended to do again is noted in my narrative reports is I referenced a large documents or collections that I reviewed and I extensively cite to the documents that I'm talking about in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I take from your answer, sir, that not every document that you would have looked at or consulted can be found in the reports that you've drafted, cited?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sir, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to know from you how it was that the documents would be selected to be processed or reviewed by you, and what I mean by that is did other Prosecution staff come to you with documents that they had preselected for your review or did you go through the corpus of documentation to select and find documents to analyse?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the latter. It was my office, the military analyst team, that had first crack at the documents, as it were, following the searches of the Zvornik and the Bratunac Brigade. It was our team's responsibility to go through all of the single documents -- all of the documents in both particular collections as well as the Krajina Corps collection which we obtained at the same time, and the first line of attack it was essentially make an index of the entire collection. So the military analysts did that portion. The second part obviously in looking at the documents in question, for the construction of my reports, the documents that I selected, I selected. They were not selected for me by anyone in that particular context, so I mean it's entirely my discretion as to what goes in those reports or what did not go in those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now to segue into my next set of questions I'd like to call up in e-court 1D1241 which I think we will see is a portion of the transcript from the Popovic trial, and if we can have page 18 of that document in e-court, which should correlate to transcript page 19592 of the underlying transcript. And, sir, if you could follow along with me I'd like to read back lines 2 through 8 and then ask you some follow-up questions about the testimony you gave there: "Q. All right. And how about information from the investigation? Did you have access to that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I had full access to the investigators as well as all of the facets of the investigation that was going on, certainly with respect to interviewing military personnel, interviewing police personnel, things of that nature. So I -- I had full access to all of the materials of the investigation during my time here from 1997 through 2003." Now, sir, first I have to ask you, is this selection that we've gone through together accurately recording the testimony that you gave or that you remember giving in the Popovic case on this question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it truthful?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, what I want to ask you about is did you still have full access to the materials and all facets of the OTP investigation at any time subsequent to leaving UN employment in 2003 and if so, when and why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes, sir, at least parts of the material. One of the things that the Office of the Prosecutor agreed to and permitted me was to maintain access to the EDS system which would allow me to access documents on my own as I was preparing subsequent reports or preparing for testimony here. The other practice that we normally did with the Office of the Prosecutor is that perhaps six to eight months before a projected period where I might testify, the US government would make me available and I would come here to The Hague and spend several weeks reviewing new documents, new statements, new issues like that, that have come up from the Office of the Prosecutor. So I could look at any of the new material and make an analysis as to whether or not that either confirmed previous-held opinions or views or whether this new information would cause me to modify those views.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, during that time period when you say you would come here six to eight months before your intended testimony to review new statements, new documents, new issues, that have come up from the Office of the Prosecutor, would those be selected or collated for you by the Office of the Prosecutor or would you have to search through the corpus of the documents to obtain that information and those documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- when I came here, the normal practice was Mr. McCloskey or another member of the Prosecution staff would have a bunch of documents that they would of course want me to look at. My normal practice was not only to look at those but to also go talk to the remaining military analysts who I knew handled these collections. I would normally get copies of the large spreadsheets that they had accumulated, indexing these documents, and very frequently I would ask for additional information. Same with the witness statements. So I mean, I've never felt in all my time since leaving the Tribunal that if I did not ask for a particular document or set of documents, you know, I would not be given immediate access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that for purposes of the work that you did in preparation for the Popovic trial, you did not obtain and comprehensively review all of the documents with respect to the ABiH military from the collection but, rather, limited your review for the month of July 1995 and material that you were able -- that the Office of the Prosecutor was able to obtain in a search of the 2nd Corps as well as some ABiH documents, the Zvornik Brigade of the VRS had, by virtue of their capture of some documents from the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My focus was limited to July 1995 that corresponds with the crime base as charged in the indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But my question was, sir, is it correct that you did not review all of the documentation from the ABiH military from July 1995 but, rather, limited your review to documents obtained from the 2nd Corps during an OTP search and some ABiH documents that were in the possession of the Zvornik Brigade having been captured from elements of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did review the documents of the 28th Division that were captured by the Zvornik Brigade, and I did review documents, not all of them I presume but certainly some from the ABiH, the 2nd Corps, in July of 1995. I can't tell you what documents I didn't review.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can -- strike that. Can you tell me, subsequent to your work in the Popovic case, have you undertaken to go back and review any further material from the ABiH, that is ABiH documentation, that is in the possession of the Prosecution relating to July 1995 to do a more comprehensive review?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that I didn't start the process to do that, but during my cross-examination by General Tolimir, we spent many hours reviewing ABiH documents from July 1995, so obviously I have seen them and have discussed them at some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you think discussing documents in some detail in cross-examination is equal to the type of review that you would have done had you been preparing your report, looking at the documents, cross checking them, verifying them at your leisure?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't but again I go back to my original position which is I would only spend my time and deal with issues that were relevant in the sense of Srebrenica 1995. If I've already intellectually conceded that the VRS had the military legitimate right to attack the 28th Division, the actual day-to-day combat by the 28th Division did not have relevance to what I was seeking to analyse.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, since you say that you would only spend your time with items that were relevant in the sense of Srebrenica 1995, am I correct that for purposes of your review and work for both the Popovic case in 2008 and the Perisic case in 2009 you did not have occasion to address or analyse the so-called NIOD, N-I-O-D, report of the Dutch authorities as to Srebrenica 1995 because it -- at that time it had not been translated fully from Dutch into English?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, and also, I would tell you that I also did not review that particular report because my understanding was that when I am called before this particular Tribunal and others to testify about my work, I testify about my work. I'm not here to testify about past ICTY judgements and I'm not here to testify about the NIOD report so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since portions of that report now have been translated into English, have you since that time undertaken to analyse or review the NIOD report and if so, how much of it or what portions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not, sir. I have not reviewed it. I have not analysed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is it your position that the NIOD report is not relevant material to the type of expert review that you were doing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. My position is that when I'm called to testify here I'm called to testify about my work and I don't want to be in a position of testifying about my work somehow influenced by another body of work. My analysis is limited in this respect to the military documents and what they mean in relation to the crimes as charged in 1995. It is not to do a comprehensive historical review of all things that happened in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to your work for the beginning of your tenure to the present day, would you agree with me that the -- that you have never obtained or performed -- the comprehensive corpus of the entirety of the documents from the VRS Main Staff and thus did not have the ability to analyse and review those documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this date, I am not aware that we have an entire collection of documents from the Main Staff. That is correct, sir. And when I say, "We," I mean the Office of the Prosecutor in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, for purposes of the review that you have done in all the cases here at the ICTY where you are relying on a document said to be issued by General Ratko Mladic, would you agree that most of these documents would be the teletype printed signature which would be the copy received on the receiving end of a teletype transmission rather than the original with the originating stamp and original signature of either General Mladic or whomever sent the communication under his name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I would agree or disagree, simply because I've never actually conducted that type of an analysis to determine what percentage of documents fall into either category.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. And is it correct that for purposes of preparing your reports in this case, you did not take into account or review either the SFRY constitution nor the constitution of its constituent Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I've reviewed the constitutions of either. In general I may have looked at them, but certainly for the type of analysis that I'm doing from a military context, a review of a constitution for either ABiH or the SFRY, I didn't think it was particularly useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say you didn't think it was particularly useful, was that a decision you reached or a decision that someone else within the Office of the Prosecution reached?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my decision. Obviously the constitution of the Republika Srpska and its laws would be the controlling factors, given the fact that the officers that we were looking at with respect to their potential involvement in the crimes were officers of that particular entity or state. So again it was my decision, and that's why I believed those other documents that you mentioned weren't particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your work at the Office of the Prosecutor, did you have occasion to seek the consultation of any other experts, whether military or otherwise, and whether internal to the Office of the Prosecutor or external to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, I sat in an office with eight other military analysts from various countries. I'm not sure how much they appreciated it but I certainly was willing to reach out at any opportunity to float any odd-ball idea I might have had off of them. So I had access to those individuals and their professional observations on certain issues. Until the Krstic case began and the documents began becoming public exhibits, it was a closed collection. As a result, I did not have the opportunity to consult with outside experts with respect to on a day-to-day basis. There were no outside -- if you're on staff, by definition you're not an outside expert. I was, however, during the course of the Krstic trial, able to present my work to General Dannatt, who was a military expert witness for the prosecutor in that case, and he did have the opportunity to review my narrative reports as well as the -- the narrative report and the command report that were published at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did General Dannatt have any contributions to your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Apart from the review to personnel within the military analysts office of the Office of the Prosecutor and General Dannatt that you've just testified about, did you at any time subsequent to the Krstic case submit any of the newer reports for any type of academic peer review process?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you could qualify it -- I mean I'm not an academic obviously and I don't put myself off to be one, but certainly since the publication of those original reports and subsequent reports, I've been cross-examined by 20 Defence counsel and perhaps 20 some-odd military experts, as well as six different trial panels on those particular reports, so I would qualify that as peer review on steroids. Certainly these reports are public. They have been public for over a decade now, with the exception of the Main Staff report, and there has been an enormous opportunity for a variety of people with military experience to comment on them if they choose to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did I understand you correctly that these written expert reports that we have and the drafted Srebrenica narrative that's being presented in this case, originally started off as internal aids - I think "running guides" is the term that you used - to assist Prosecution counsel and investigators to do their work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time consult or review any treatises written by others recognised as experts on the topic of the structure and functioning of the JNA or the Yugoslav All People's Defence for purposes of preparing these internal aids or running guides to assist Prosecution counsel and investigators in doing their work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, at that particular time in 1997 and 1998, it would not particularly surprise you that members of the RS or the SFRY were not exactly keen to co-operate with the Office of the Prosecutor. So we certainly did not have access to individuals from there. What I did have access to, however, was, and I did follow to some degree, other proceedings that were going on at the Tribunal, where various Defence experts who were former SFRY military officers would testify in various other cases in order to obtain snippets of information as to how the various armed forces of the warring factions were organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you say the RS and the SFRY. By that time, did you mean the FRY?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that would be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia? Did you have good co-operation at the Office of the Prosecutor with the military libraries in those countries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were able from the ABiH to obtain former JNA documents from their military library which many of them were translated and used by me. For obvious reasons, we did not go to ABiH military officers to try and explain VRS military doctrine or tactics. So, again, we had a broad collection of the doctrinal and regulatory material that was provided by various countries. We did not avail ourselves to using ABiH or Macedonian officers in that respect or Croatian officers to explain, at least to the Srebrenica trial team, how the VRS may or may not have worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we are not understanding each other, sir. I asked you about treatises written, contained in libraries as to the JNA and the Yugoslav All People's Defence system that would have been available in Croatia, in Slovenia, in Macedonia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina dating from before the conflict that would have discussed the types of structures that you were tasked with reviewing to determine if the VRS operated under those same rules, regulations and doctrine.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't need to see that material, simply because once we had the basic JNA rules and regulations that we were able to obtain and we had them translated, we can do that analysis ourself. So generally speaking, I mean, the only treatises or expert papers that I recall I did read would be those papers relating to the SFRY and some analysis by their legal branch as to the recent publication of the rules on the law of land warfare and how they applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'm curious. How does this process work? Who is it at the military analysts' office that decides we are going to look at this treatise or document but we are not going to be concerned with any others, we are not going to seek out the existence of any others? How does that decision making process work? How do you know what is relevant to look at, what is germane to look at, and what is considered to be authoritative on the subject that you're looking at, if all you're taking is the documents translating them and reviewing them without relating to prior treatises done by professionals in -- who studied the forces of the JNA and the All People's Defence system for an extensive period of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have a foundation of what treatises he's talking about? I'm not aware of any and we are creating this -- this -- perhaps it's real, perhaps it's a fiction, but what treatises is he not reviewing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're reviewing to what the witness may have missed. Could you give him any clue as to what he may have overlooked so as a basis for this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's my understanding that multiple books and publications from the formation of the JNA through its demise were written and are contained in all the libraries of the former Yugoslav republics. If he looked and he knows what is out there then he can choose what he can look at and what he cannot look at. Our position is that they did not even seek those out, so I don't think they are giving any kind of titles to this gentleman -- will assist him in refreshing his recollection but he's quite capable of answering and telling me whether I'm correct in my assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question but I express as a concern at this moment that we are dealing with all these matters on a level of abstraction which might not bring us very much, and does not touch upon the substance of what the witness testified about, which is of equal if not more importance to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before he answers the question I have a question to the witness myself. Mr. Butler, in your brief that you were given by the OTP, was it ever part of your task to review these treatises that are being referred to in order to determine if the VRS operated under those -- the same rules and regulations and doctrine of the various countries that have been mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can answer both questions at once, sir. Given the fact that the VRS was created in 1992, I did not particularly think that more abstract writings on various JNA topics in the 1970s or 1980s was particularly relevant to that. The question at hand was whether or not the VRS, as constituted in 1992, was following the broader rules and regulations of the former JNA and applying those in their daily activities and in their combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And my question is: Were you tasked with making the determination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was tasked with making the determination whether or not VRS was operating in a similar manner to the JNA in accordance with their rules. I don't recall if it's by the Prosecution, but certainly I knew I had to accomplish that mission in order to go further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can get back to these original internal aids or running guides that you drafted for the assistance of Prosecution personnel that eventually led to the drafting of the expert reports, do you still have those original written documents that were running guides for the Prosecution and, if so, do you have a problem with them being disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly don't have copies of those early initial versions. They were on the -- if they still exist, they -- there may be electronic copies of them on the share drive. I don't know whether or not they have been disclosed or are disclosable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were these early writings by you for the assistance of Prosecution staff distributed only within the Office of the Prosecutor or were they distributed to others at the Tribunal for their information and potential use?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distribution of that material at that time was limited to individuals of the Office of the Prosecutor only, and the specific investigation teams that needed them. I don't know who at that time outside the Office of the Prosecutor would have had any interest in looking at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how about your superiors at the US armed forcers while you were still employed by them? Were you provided copies -- were they provided copies of these?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that they would definitely fall in the category of people who had no interest of what I was writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you have been listed as a Rule 70 witness as in prior trials and in the past there has been counsel from the US embassy in court, so I do have to ask you, for purposes of the work that you did, did you utilise any information or perhaps intelligence resources of the United States or its armed forces in preparing your reports which would not have originated from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did the United States of America or personnel of the US armed forces have a role in approving or vetting the final reports that we now have before us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that would go back to -- again that would imply they actually cared at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to take you back to that point in time during your tenure at the Office of the Prosecutor to find out when it was that the -- or how it came about that the decision was made to transform this prior work into an expert report and then to change you from an analyst to a potential expert witness to be used as evidence before the Trial Chambers.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you want me to explain it in a running narrative or were you going to ask me a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was going to ask you a question. How and when did that decision become made, and who made it? Did you propose it to the Prosecution or did the Prosecution counsel propose it to you? That's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, sometime after General Krstic was arrested and we were in a pre-trial phase, there was discussions as to whether or not -- or maybe not whether or not but probably more accurately how the Office of the Prosecutor could effectively explain in some context what the military documents meant with respect to then General Krstic. The various Prosecutors, and certainly it wasn't a unanimous decision, did come to the conclusion that the best way to do that would be to essentially have me publish those reports that I had created as internal aids and testify behind them as a way of allowing the Court to understand what all of the military documents meant in context to the crime scenes and other military activities that were going on. So it was only after General Krstic had been apprehended and we were preparing to go to trial that that decision was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that during the first several years that you were at the Office of the Prosecutor, during the time period when you were still an active duty army officer, at that time, you were salaried and paid by the US army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the time that you were still being paid by the United States Army as an active duty army officer, but were on loan to the Office of the Prosecutor, did you perform any additional duties for the US army or was your work entirely for the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Once when I was loaned to the Office of the Prosecutor or seconded, I took all of my tasking from them, them being the Office of the Prosecutor and the ICTY. I had no other additional duties with the United States Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if you could tie that together with the answer you gave as to when you would have been transformed into an expert, during the time period that were you salaried by the US army were you at that time already acting as an expert or did that take place sometime later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the -- my official title as an individual who was seconded like anybody else in the UN system was expert on mission. I was acting as a military analyst like the other military analysts for the Office of the Prosecutor. We certainly never called ourselves military experts per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned other military analysts for the Office of the Prosecutor. Are you familiar with an individual by the name of Mr. Philip Coo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was he a colleague of yours at the military analysts office at the Office of the Prosecutor doing similar work as your own, analysing military documents and seeking to testify as an expert in court about the same?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Coo was a military analyst who came years after I did. He was working on a different set of cases. I -- again because of the fact that I was working Bosnian Serb related cases and he was working different cases, I don't know of the specifics of what the team that he was working for had an intention with him to testify or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that two Trial Chambers in the Milutinovic case and the Djordjevic case declined to treat Mr. Coo as an expert because his methodology of analysis of military documents and giving the meaning of the same would infringe upon the Chamber's domain of assessing the documents and evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I was aware that at one point I think that there was an application out for him to testify. I don't recall I ever knew of the ultimate decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then I'll move on. Now, I don't propose to go through your CV with any great amount of detail but I would like to ask you about some of your experience, in particular especially matters that are not reflected in your CS, such as your formal education, for one. I'd like to go back to the time period before the ICTY and, first of all, why don't you tell us in relation to your formal education, am I correct that your college degree was a bachelor's degree in political science at the European division of the University of Maryland earned as part-time evening student while were you simultaneously serving in the US armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if any of your course work towards this degree involved any studies of the framework of the state of Yugoslavia or its armed forces system or its national defence doctrine?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now then I want to move on away from your education to your work in the US army. First of all, can you tell me if you attended courses at or earned degrees at any military schools or academies and, if so, what field your course of study was in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As my resume notes, I did attend the military intelligence warrant officer basic and advanced courses at Fort Huachuca. I passed those courses successfully and have certificates related to that, but it is not a military academy per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think -- well, just to verify and that those courses would not have dealt with the state of Yugoslavia or its armed forces or the national defence doctrine as part of their curriculum?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to focus on your actual duties, duty posts within the US army. First of all, am I correct that your first operational assignment started in January of 1982 and lasted until 1985 when you were assigned to a military intelligence group in Europe?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, from January of 1982 to July of 1985, I was assigned to the 66th military intelligence group, at that time stationed in Munich, Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During your time from 1982 to 1985, with the 66th military intelligence group, did have you any duties involving work in relation to or exposure to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, its armed forces or its national defence doctrine?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After that you were deployed to Texas for sometime and eventually transferred to the United States central command where for two years you studied the Soviet army operations in Afghanistan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you at that time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down please for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you during that time at the central command have any duties researching or studying the JNA for any purposes whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that you did a second tour of duty in Europe after being made a warrant officer, being assigned to the all-source production section of the 3rd infantry division in Wurzburg, Germany?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at that time, did any of your work involve collecting intelligence on or studying the state of Yugoslavia or its armed forces or national defence doctrine?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, for a several month period at the end of that, I did look a little bit into Yugoslavia. At that time, in 1992, or 1991 and 1992, there was some discussion of a European rapid reaction force potentially deploying to the former Yugoslavia and as a part of the US component of that, the 3rd Infantry Division was assigned to start potentially looking at military options and obviously supporting the intelligence portion of that, I did have to start making myself aware of general aspects of the ongoing conflict. Having said that, it did not include an in-depth analytical review of the Yugoslav National Army, All People's Defence, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've said that there was discussion of a quote/unquote "European rapid reaction force." Did you mean to say that there was contingency planning going on with respect to the possibility of NATO forces being deployed to Bosnia in some form or fashion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it wasn't necessarily NATO. It was still this thing called the Western European union and a European rapid reaction force that was supposedly being put together for it. There was a US component but it -- as it was designed, it was supposed to operate outside of NATO. I think as history notes it wasn't a particularly successful military cohesive body, and as a result everything kind of fell back on NATO again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So was the contingency planning foreseeing the Western European union or NATO action in Bosnia, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I was there it was a WEU, as I recall. It may have transitioned to NATO sometime in 1992 but by then I was already leaving the division and going on to my next assignment, so I don't know any of those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up in e-court 1D1241 and page 12 in e-court. It should correlate to transcript page 19586 from the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to review with you, sir, the answer you give starting at line 2 on this page, and if you could follow along I'll have some questions for you: "A. After finishing up with my assignment in south-west Asia, with US 7th Corps, doing what is now known, I guess, as the first Gulf War, I reverted back to my original position in 3rd Infantry Division in Wurzburg, Germany. At that time it was early 1992 and as part of NATO, and part of the central army group, there was contingency planning going on with respect to the possibility of NATO forces being deployed to Bosnia in some form or fashion." Does that refresh your recollection, sir, if the work you did was specifically geared towards having NATO intervention in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, yes, sir, I mean obviously my mind is playing a little trick on me. It's been 20 years since that period of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn or focus on line 24 of this transcript and go on to the next page, I'd like to explore the types of sources that you reviewed at that time to plan the contingencies of NATO involvement: "We were not engaged in a day-to-day monitoring of the military activities of any of the warring parties, if that's what you're getting at." If we go to the next page: "Q. Any general materials for historical background? "A. At that time it would probably be whatever news and media reports were coming out of Yugoslavia. I guess it's a matter of fact at this point that certainly when the civil conflict in Bosnia started, it wasn't a primary focus of the United States." Sir, is this a fair and accurate rendition of the testimony you gave as to the types of sources that you looked at during this time in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We -- Yugoslavia was not of intelligence collection priority of the United States at that time, and therefore most of the information that we were receiving about the warring parties and the conflict in general was a result of open-source information generally from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as part of the work that you were doing during this time period, potentially to support a deployment of NATO and US troops to Bosnia, can you tell us were you preparing, participating in any contingencies to have NATO forces intervene or act militarily against the Army of the Republika Srpska or any Serb structures?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Simply from our perspective, what we were doing at the division level was trying to assemble basic information with respect to the terrain, the road network, those general pieces of information that a military force would have to know in order to move or garrison in an area, things of that nature, rail movement issues to move the division if possible. I don't recall that I ever participated in any meeting or did any work with respect in 1992 with respect to any mission planning for combat activities against anybody in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This would be a good time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. By the way, Mr. McCloskey, we still need to find time to accomplish what we started, that is to receive the comments of the witness on the list of, I think on documents, which he may have consulted. That's still to be done. I would rather do it than later today. Or, Mr. Ivetic, if this would be a suitable moment to hear from him on that matter first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why don't we do it now before we lose sight of it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, before we continue the cross-examination, there was an outstanding issue that is you giving some comments on a list of documents which were -- you were invited to review. Are you ready to do it at this moment or would you rather take your time in the next break to look at them again and then answer any questions in relation to those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm prepared to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. McCloskey, what we asked, more or less, is to look at the documents and I think that you would comment on whether you had reviewed them while preparing your reports. That was the main question, I think. And then do you have the list before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think the first one was 65 ter 05385.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any comment on whether you reviewed it, any further comments on the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I have reviewed that document. When I look at these documents I recognise many of them from not only my review but I believe I also testified about them in the Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do the parties -- do you have a similar report for all of the documents or are there some which receive a different report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, there are a total of 16 documents that are highlighted in yellow, three of which have exhibit numbers but the remaining 13, the report is the same, I have reviewed the particular document and in most cases I recall testifying about this particular document in another context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further questions on these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think a list has been prepared. Madam Registrar is then invited to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will prepare a list of the documents and provisionally assign numbers so that we can decide on admission. Then, Mr. Ivetic, having dealt with this matter, you may proceed. You may continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to focus back again on this time period in August of 1992, when you were working with the -- with the 3rd Infantry Division in Germany, working on contingency plans for NATO intervention in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You've mentioned the open intelligence sources that were you looking at. Did your work deal with the results of any HUMINT from covert operatives already on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the work or the contingencies that were being worked on for purposes of this time period, was it foreseen that NATO or US forces would militarily intervene or act against the Bosnian Muslim armed forces or the Croats, or were those factions considered to be blue or friendly forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this gentleman is here as an expert witness, not as a fact witness, so to delve into the reliability, independence and ability of someone to be an expert it would be important to know whether they were a -- involved in any way preceding the party that they are providing expertise upon as an enemy and if they had any allegiance during the conflict. The jurisprudence this Tribunal has disqualified persons who did have a role as an opposing force and so I'm quite entitled, I think, to ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: However, your question was whether it was foreseen. You did not ask the witness anything about his personal involvement in that. So that's commenting on what others may have foreseen. Would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the work that you did on these contingencies for NATO to intervene in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were the Bosnian Muslim armed forces and the Croat forces designated as blue or friendly forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The work that I did was simply trying to assemble information with respect to how the division could move from where it was currently garrisoned in Germany to the effected region. If work like that was being done by NATO staff, I mean, I wasn't a part of it and we didn't see any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, at transcript page 16113 of last week's transcript, you indicated your role as being to advise your commander what an armed adversary is doing and assist him in their goal of defeating said armed adversary. In the context of the contingency planning that you were doing in August of 1992, did you at that time consider the Army of Republika Srpska to be an armed adversary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. We didn't consider anyone to be an armed adversary. I believe that the assumption was that if NATO did deploy there and I don't know under what circumstances they were thinking about, that it would be as a peacekeeping force, not as a party to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did any of your work whilst at the United States Army involve planning the contingency of NATO or US forces clandestinely arming the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Croat factions in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could just focus again on the last part of that testimony that's still on the screen in front of us, when you say that the types of materials that were used for this work were primarily news and media reports coming out of Yugoslavia, would those have been media and news reports of the domestic former Yugoslav news agencies or of international news agencies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been whatever information we could have laid our hands on at the time. Again, as I indicated, Yugoslavia, the Balkans region was not an intelligence collection priority of the United States at the time, certainly not the United States Army in Europe. And as a result, we found ourselves having very little information of usable value during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that what you've just described as fairly standard operating procedure when you come to a situation where you don't have already-developed dossiers that you try to get your -- lay your hands on everything you can about the topic, as a military analyst working in your field?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was that done when you commenced your work for the Office of the Prosecutor for purposes of generating the reports that you subsequently authored?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the sense that when I was doing my initial research, I tried to obtain material obviously translated in English that would be useful for me to conduct my overall analysis. I tried to lay my hands on whatever I thought would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, could Mr. Mladic lower the volume of his voice. Mr. Ivetic, when you referred to transcript page 16113 and talked about an armed adversary, may I take it that you wanted to refer to a potential armed adversary --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as the language?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I misspoke if I did not include that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to move to your training and experience. First of all, prior to the Office of the Prosecutor am I correct you had no education or background in law or law enforcement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. Prior to my coming to the ICTY, I -- my career pattern was strictly military intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as a US army intelligence officer, you were forbidden by law from having been -- from being involved in any criminal investigatory work by virtue of your position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At the time that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you essentially learned techniques and tactics while you were dealing with the law enforcement personnel and lawyers at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily learned techniques and tactics, but I certainly had to adapt the techniques and tactics and methodologies that I would traditionally use in a military intelligence sense in order to satisfy my customers, which in this case were investigators and lawyers, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say to satisfy your customers, that would be the Office of the Prosecutor, that would be lawyers and investigators within the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, at the early stages of my work, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take a look at 1D1260 with you, and page 35 of the same in e-court, which should correlate to transcript page 20155 of the Popovic transcript. And the part I want to focus on with you is in the beginning of the first dozen lines. And if you could again follow along with me, sir: "Q. Tell me what those techniques and tactics were that you learned with respect to dealing with law enforcement since you had no education and experience in those areas prior to that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by virtue of having access to not only a world-class body of lawyers but also investigators from both common law and civil law backgrounds, what I was able to do is, by watching them work, looking at what they were doing, and what they were trying to accomplish with respect to their own investigations, it gave me the foundation to be able to look at what types of military information they would need to support their investigative processes. "Q. I honestly don't know if I understand you. Was that a technique or a tactic that you explained to me? "A. That would be a combination of both." First of all, sir, does this accurately describe or depict your testimony describing the process by which you learned techniques and tactics whilst at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, learned or modified, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say that you were looking at what the Prosecution staff were trying to accomplish, and that this gave you the information you needed to know what type of military information they would need to support their investigative process, am I correct that you also wanted to provide them with military information that would let them successfully accomplish their purpose of prosecuting persons for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would walk it back from prosecute and certainly acknowledge in the early years I wanted them to be able obviously to successfully investigate these crimes. So clearly for the first two and a half years of my tenure here, one of the things I was very focused on doing working with the investigators and lawyers was, again, as part of a joint process, figuring out all of the facts related to the Srebrenica crime base, how they lined up and identifying individuals who were potentially responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you "say figuring out all of the facts relating to the Srebrenica crime base" but you limited yourself to just the documentation that the Office of the Prosecutor had and did not look beyond that to NIOD or any other compendiums of information about fact relating to Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is inferring that NIOD existed at these early days which Mr. Butler is talking about and that would be not true so I -- please, inferences like that are inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I would like to add that the purpose of what you're doing and the sources you were doing for that purpose are two different matters and they should be clearly distinguished. I think both may deserve attention but they are not to be mixed up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've mentioned a couple times today the Yugoslav national defence doctrine. Would you agree with me and have you understood that we have been talking about what is referred to in the vernacular in the former Yugoslavia as the quote/end quote "All People's Defence"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In that regard, I believe you conceded in the Popovic trial at transcript page 20565, lines 18 through 20, that you don't pretend to be an expert on the issues of the All People's Defence doctrine. Do you still hold that position or concession?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we get the page on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can. If we go to 1D1246. And page 61 of that document should correlate to transcript page 20565, and lines 18 through 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And perhaps since we have it up on the screen, sir, I'll read it into the record and then ask you to confirm it: "Q. Have you studied the concept of All People's Defence once you had finished at the OTP? "A. No. And I don't -- I don't pretend to be an expert on the issue of All People's Defence." Sir, does this transcript selection accurately report the testimony that you remember giving in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it truthful?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it still accurate that you still do not consider yourself to be an expert on All People's Defence of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, would you agree with me that both the JNA and the VRS had within their composition units that were referred to as belonging to the regiment echelon both of the artillery and infantry type, albeit they were more common in the JNA prior to 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the JNA didn't exist in 1995. The former JNA did in the late 1980s, early 1990s have regiments as their primary subordinate formation for divisions. There may have been one or two units still organised as regiments or called regiments in the VRS but I don't believe that was common by any stretch, in 1995, particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that you have not in fact done much research on regimental rules or regimental formations as either under the JNA or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, the Drina Corps in 1995, to my knowledge, did not have regiments and was not organised in a regimental system. So while I recall back in the day probably going through the JNA rules on regiments that we had, it didn't seem particularly relevant to what I was looking at in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But there was a 65th Protection Regiment in the VRS, was there not --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- operating in Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you hold yourself out as an expert on the topic of regiments in the VRS in terms of their structure, what rules they operated under, and so forth, or would you be reticent to do so given your lack of research on the topic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, before I started testifying with respect to much of the internal processes of a regimental organisation, I'd like to refresh my memory on some of the regimental materials, but with respect to other aspects of the 65th Protection Regiment, obviously I have testified to those, how they relate to command and control and other issues, and I'm comfortable in that realm because they followed the normal command and staff processes. So I guess my answer is it will be on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you consider or hold yourself out as an expert as to those items relating to regiments in the VRS that you have testified about or have mentioned in your reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I never hold myself out to be an expert on any of these particular issues. I, as a military intelligence officer, I'm an intelligence technician. This is what I do as a profession. I'm not a classical academic expert in that sense. However, obviously, if it is in my reports or if I have testified about it, I feel secure in my knowledge of those issues to be able to discuss them before this Trial Chamber and defend them as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are one of those areas that you did review and spend considerable time upon that you feel secure in your knowledge of that issue, would one of those areas be the rules of service of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, those are referenced in my Command Responsibility Reports, those are the rules of service. I think they are dated, if memory serves, sometime late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In that regard I'd like to look at 1D1263 with you, and page 64 of the same, which should correlate to transcript page 20826 of the Popovic case, I think it is. Yes. And I'd like to go through lines 7 through 17 with you, sir, and ask you some follow-up questions: "Q. Now, before we move on to the questions, these rules are rules of the -- the rules of service of the Army of Republika Srpska. "A. Yes, sir. "Q. And if the average battalion soldier was aware of anything, these are the rules he's likely to be aware of, aren't they? "A. Yes, sir. "Q. And just to complete the picture, these rules were in force in 1995 and carried on being in force until they were revoked in 1997. Did you know that? "A. I wasn't aware when they were revoked, but I certainly knew they were in force during the period that we are talking about." Does this selection accurately depict the testimony that you gave in the Popovic case?"

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is this the kind of thing that you would think would be germane to your analysis and review to know when the main documents that you are relying upon, when they were issued, when they were revoked or superseded, wouldn't those be the basic elementary tasks of an expert such as yourself conducting the type of review that you were conducting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And what I was taking issue here was the fact that he used the terminology "revoked." My understanding is that those particular rules were in fact superseded in 1997. The fact that they were superseded in 1997, while interesting, had no bearing on what was happening in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to move on to another topic. In the course of the time period that you were at the Office of the Prosecutor, I would like to know precisely how many total interviews you conducted or were present for of VRS personnel in relation to the Srebrenica component of the case, of their case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to remember -- at least give a ballpark estimate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me help you out on that. I can refresh your recollection, sir. If we can have 1D1241 in e-court, and it should be page 21 of the same and that should correlate to page 19595 of, again, the Popovic transcript, just a different day, and lines 11 through 25 which I would like to read with you, sir, to refresh your recollection. If I may just switch microphones so it's easier. And I quote from line 11: "A. When we started getting access to military officers of the VRS to be able to interview them, I started to participate in those interviews in order to assist the investigators and whatever lawyers were there with understanding some of the answers of the accused with respect to the context of the JNA, as well as to pose my own questions to either confirm or deny our working thesis at the time that the rules, the regulations and the procedures of the JNA were, in fact, followed by the VRS. "Q. So did you actually question some witnesses? "A. Yes, sir, I did. "Q. Do you have -- can you give us a rough number? "A. For the OTP, I probably personally participated in many -- in maybe 24, 25, two dozen. I mean, I think there are about three separate missions where I participated in direct interviews, and in those missions where I didn't participate in direct interviews because I had other commitments to do, I certainly read the transcripts of the interviews afterwards." Now, sir, first of all, we can discard with my prior question and just deal with this. Does this accurately reflect the testimony as you recall giving it in the prior proceeding as to the interviews that you would have directly participated in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did any of the 24 to 25 or perhaps two dozen interviews that you directly participated in involve any members of the VRS Main Staff and, if so, what individuals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Bogdan Sladojevic at that time, who was then general; Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic; I had an opportunity -- obviously I did interview or at least have a discussion with General Milovanovic. Those are the ones that are coming to memory now, that I personally participated in. There may have been other interviews where I just read the transcripts afterwards but those are three that at least at the moment I recall participating in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to these three now, when would those interviews have taken place? Would they have been early in your work? Would they have been later in your work? Is there any way you can give us some idea of when that would have been without of course giving -- I don't expect precise dates and time but --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I think those particular interviews took place in the period between the Krstic trial and the Blagojevic and Jokic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'm going to have to ask you to explain, you, I believe, used the terminology of saying that you did an interview or at least have a discussion with General Milovanovic. Could you please clarify what exactly was the nature of your contact with General Manojlo Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall at the time that General Milovanovic had contacted the Office of the Prosecutor and wanted to reach out to the Office of the Prosecutor, and to make contact with him to discuss some issues related to Srebrenica. I accompanied team leader Jean-Rene Ruez to Banja Luka, where we had a meeting with him. It was not an interview per se. There was not notes taken, at least by me. I can't tell you this day what notes, if any, Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez may have taken. I'm not sure if it was considered to be off the record or not, the discussion. But we did spend an hour and a half with him discussing issues related to the broader aspect of Srebrenica, the broader aspects of some of the VRS in July of 1995, and what he was doing in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say there were not any notes taken, at least by me, do you know if the encounter with General Milovanovic was recorded or memorialised by any recording equipment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have -- I don't believe we had an audiotape recorder, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or video for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else in the meeting appear to be taking notes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I didn't. I don't recall if Jean-Rene did. I certainly don't recall if the general himself was taking notes or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else present for this meeting, apart from the three of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our team interpreter was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you feel -- do you recall the identity of the team interpreter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I think the policy when we talk about interpreters we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Or perhaps we can have a -- is that -- is that -- can we do that maybe outside of court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please, if we can just do private session, I think that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to these 24, 25 or perhaps two dozen interviews that you directly participated in, are you able to give us a breakdown of what percentage would have been with VRS personnel on the one hand as opposed to Army of BiH or non-VRS personnel on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that I am talking about, where I say the 24 or 25, are all VRS personnel. I recall only participating in discussions with perhaps one or two ABiH military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during those interviews, how many of the interviews were of persons who were considered at the time or at least given the warning at the time that they were suspects under investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I couldn't tell you the percentage breakdown. Some of the interviews were interviews where we were required to warn the individuals they were suspects. Some of them were not, and they were considered to be simply witnesses. I just -- I can't off-hand tell you what the percentage breakdown is. I just don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall in relation to the discussion that you had -- that you and Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez had with Mr. Milovanovic, whether on or off the record, was he a suspect at that time that you had that discussion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, he was not. I mean we had already been able, as far as our investigation was concerned, given his location and his activities in the western Krajina region, and from the information that we had available at the time, he was not considered to be a suspect with respect to the events of Srebrenica in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now, in relation to these 24 or 25 interviews, did you in all of them actually pose questions as opposed to just giving advice to the other Prosecution staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many of the interviews I was invited to pose questions, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to those interviews, were there occasions where you had to provide guidance to the Prosecution staff that were asking questions including guidance on proposing questions for them to pose to the interviewee?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Particularly when it came with respect to a technical issue on applications of command or applications of the security branch or certain other applications of, you know, technical staff officers, I would discuss with the -- with the investigator, if he was leading the interview, what issues that I would like explored and more importantly give him enough background so that he would understand or she would understand the answer that that officer would presumably give back.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
