utterances.text: Now, when you say you -- what issues you would like explored, were you directing the investigators in the work of their interview? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The interviews were always conducted under the leadership of the investigator. Again, I provide technical advice and assistance. If we are interviewing somebody who was a logistics officer in a particular unit, as you might expect, you know, a police investigator is not going to have a really broad base of knowledge on convoy operations of an armed force, you know, and the rules and regulations pertaining to that. So again my role was to work with those investigators so they would be able to ask pertinent questions, understand the answers that were received back by them, and if I was in the room, if I had to clarify any particular issues, I did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you for purposes of these 24 to 25 interviews you participated in meet with Prosecution personnel before the interview to discuss strategy with them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a normal process of our interviews that we did at the time, we would meet in advance, we would discuss the strategy in the sense of what issues we wanted to explore with a particular witness. We would also obviously acquaint ourselves whether or not the individual was being interviewed as a witness or as a suspect. That was a normal practice, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you have been involved in such strategy meetings as part of the normal process even for those interviews that you did not personally directly participate in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend. I mean, there were -- obviously there were interviews going on along a wide range of issues. If one of the investigators who was going, you know, from The Hague to Bosnia was going to interview a VRS military officer, it would be customary that they would approach me or the other military analysts who were supporting the Srebrenica team at the time, and ask basic information about, you know, what documents that we had about an individual's potential role in the VRS, what questions we might want asked or answered regarding some question that we would have as military analysts. So, again, we were a resource that the investigators could utilise to prepare ultimately for their interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As part of this process or normal procedure that you've just now described for us, did you have a role in suggesting what individuals should be sought to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that I was part of meetings where decisions -- where we would nominate individuals who we wanted to interview for various purposes, be they suspects or witnesses, from a military perspective, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about at trial? Did you have any role whatsoever in the selection of witnesses slated to testify for the Prosecution at any trials? And if so, on how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it were to happen that way, it would only be obviously during my tenure here so it would cover only the Krstic case and the Blagojevic and Jokic case, and with respect to that, I mean, Mr. McCloskey and the other lawyers always gave me a voice at the table when discussing some of these issues, but at the end of the day it was the decision of the Prosecutors who were trying the case which witnesses to call and under what circumstances. So, again, in my role, advising them of what information we had with respect to various people, what the expectation or the anticipation of that they might testify based on what we understood of their military role in a particular issue, again, that was part of servicing the customer, so to speak, from an intelligence perspective, giving them as much information as possible in order to make the best-informed decision. So again I always had a voice at the table, but at the end of the day those decisions were made by the prosecutor, not by me or any other military analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have a voice at the table, and was it part of servicing the customer, to partake in discussions as to what witnesses should not be led at trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That -- that part wasn't my responsibility, to advise anybody what witnesses not hear from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in the proofing of any witnesses that appeared for the Prosecution in any of those trials? Again while you were still here, from up to 2003.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall participating directly in the proofing. If I did, obviously, it would be in the proofing notes, which I assume you have access to. What would normally happen in those particular cases is that during or after a proofing session, I might be asked questions from a prosecutor or another lawyer dealing with the case with respect to, This is what a particular witness said, do we have documents which will confirm or deny that particular statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to move to a somewhat related topic, the investigations themselves. To do so I propose to review a statement you made or -- in the Popovic trial. If I could have 1D1261 in e-court, page 17 of the document in e-court, which should be page 20367 of that trial's trial record, from line 12 onwards. And again, sir, I invite you to follow along and listen carefully to the questions that I pose afterwards: "Q. And I suggest to you that initially the plan was for them, 'them,' them being the lawyers and the Prosecutors, to go to you, but in your case the relationship was reversed and you went to them and you told them how this investigation would be conducted. Would that be a fair statement? "A. Within a refined avenue, I'm not sure how it works in other militaries, but in the United States military, intelligence is a customer service enterprise. We are expected and trained to be able to push information to our relative commanders. In the context that I was working, you know, the investigative team and the lawyers therein were my designated commanders. I would provide intelligence product to them in the form of my analysis and opinions and I would make recommendations as to avenues that I felt the investigators should pursue with respect to individual -- well, not only individuals, but areas that we wanted to be able to confirm or deny, not only with respect to military issues but crime-base issues. So in that respect, you know, I had the lane I was responsible for and I walked down it." Sir, does this selection that I've read for you accurately record the testimony you recall giving on this topic during the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you testify the same way if asked this same question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The fact is that with respect to particularly the early Krstic and Blagojevic and even the later trials, we collectively, the Office of the Prosecutor, were dealing with very many technical military issues involving things like the chain of command, the role and functions of the security branches, and things of that nature. So I was very active with respect to advising the lawyers and the investigators on issues relating to who needed to be interviewed in order to be able to provide information on those particular topics. You're not going to get the type of information that you're looking for about the chain of command by interviewing victims of an atrocity. So my goal, you know, and my job was to be able to overlay the military context of the Drina Corps, the Republika Srpska police, and other units that were involved in what happened in July of 1995, to allow for those issues to be appropriately investigated by the investigators and the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to focus for a bit on the methodology that you employed while at the Office of the Prosecutor and some of the material that you did have at your disposal. Now, in relation to your review of JNA material, we've talked generally about it. I'd like to get very specific. Would it be very fair -- would it be fair to say that the documents relating to JNA publications that you had access to in doing your work were only documents from the former JNA 4th Corps and 17th Corps which you then utilised as a model to determine whether or not the VRS was organised along the same lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially that is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, first of all, why don't you go ahead and explain for me your qualification of initially that is correct. When did it become different?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What became different is obviously our access to more documents. At some point we received documents from the 2nd Military District or some 2nd Military District-related documents. We had access to something known as the 5th Corps collection which were VRS documents captured by the ABiH 5th Corps in July 1995. And then of course later on down the line, we were able to confirm -- we had access to the Zvornik, Bratunac Brigade and Krajina Corps documents, and again, as time continues on, the Office of the Prosecutor gets more and more information. But in the very early stages of my analysis, I had to rely on the existing material, which was the JNA 4th Corps and 17th Corps material in order to lay out my initial thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to tie this in with something you said earlier today. Am I correct that the material you were relying upon to lay out your initial thesis from the 4th Corps, 17th Corps, 2nd Military District of the JNA, all were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by the Armija BiH, that is by the opponents of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume they were, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to actually focus for a bit on your actual work product.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see we are at the time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move to the next subject matter, we should take a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I put the following on the record: On the 6th of September of this year, the Chamber issued its decision on the 11th Rule 92 bis motion. There was a slight typographical error in the disposition where the Registry was instructed to lift the confidentiality of certain evidence. That instruction refers to the admitted evidence of witnesses RM219, RM298, and RM300. And not, as indicated erroneously, to the evidence of witness RM247 and witness RM336.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I propose now to look at something from your testimony in the Perisic case about the reports that you offered -- that you authored and which are being offered here today. If we could turn to document 1D1240 in e-court, and thereafter turn to page 51 of this document. It should be transcript page 6271 of the underlying transcript, if we could scroll up just for a little bit, I think -- the 2721 of the underlying transcript. If we could focus on line 13, please, and again, sir, I invite you to follow along and then pay attention to my questions. For purposes of background, this is where you were being asked about some corrections to your reports and language issues raised in relation to the same: "Q. With regard to these issues, and the only reason I'm asking the question is because when we started your testimony you were kind enough to correct a discrete portion of your report by deleting some language in a footnote so that your report would be technically accurate. "A. Yes, sir, but I'm operating under the assumption that everybody has my prior transcripts and all the prior corrections that have been made over the course of trials on this and that the corrections that I made was one that had not been caught previously. "Q. I see. So apart from what I have just noted, then, any other corrections to be made to your report are, as you put it, to be found in your prior testimony? "A. Yes, sir. I believe there were a couple of identified footnote citations and things of that nature that were either transposed or in the wrong location. And I think we have dealt with them as part of my prior testimony, yes, sir. "Q. With regard to your testimony here, however, we have not had the benefit of those corrections; correct? I don't mean here today, I mean just since the time you have been with us. "A. Again, like I said, they are all former transcripts. I don't know what has gone by with regard to that." Now, Mr. Butler, is this prior testimony from Perisic both accurate and indeed truthful such that you would again testify the same way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, I am aware that as a component of the reports, we discovered through time that some of the hyperlinked footnote translations don't correspond to the document that I cite. Things of that nature. Again there are also in some cases variations in translation between one Trial Chamber and another on how a document is. You know, again I accept the fact that these reports with respect to the Srebrenica narrative, the brigade command report and the corps command report, you know, have not been updated by me in writing since 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you, or has anyone gone throughout prior transcripts to at least locate and identify all of the corrections that you did make during all these prior trials, such that the report could be updated -- or the reports, I should say, could be updated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not. I don't know what the Office of the Prosecutor has done with respect to that. Certainly I know that the Defence counsel is usually diligent about picking out anything that they think is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, would it be wise to ask the Prosecution whether any such exercise has been done or whether they are willing to do the exercise, that is to point at corrections made during testimony, I'm talking about correction, not interpretations, corrections made and then to give us the portions of the documents to which these corrections apply?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, as you can imagine, I over the years always review Mr. Butler's testimony in preparing for the next trial, and I do not recall any significant changes we felt the need to make regarding a potential typo or -- when he's talking about hyperlinked what he -- there was a CD product that Mr. Ivetic has that is the reports where the footnotes -- many of them are hyperlinked. You click on them and a document pops up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We know what a hyperlink is, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In this context some of the documents that he cites are hyperlinked, or many of them, and what he's just said is sometimes there has been the wrong one. This is not the kind of thing we felt needed to be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the brief answer is that you have not systematically done such an exercise and that you felt there was no need to do that because there was nothing significant to be corrected and that you admit that there may be small mistakes here and there. Is that the short summary of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't argue with that summary, no. I might be considered more systematic than you might but, no, I think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can turn to 1D1261, and page 23 of the same, which ought to correlate to transcript page 20373 of the -- I think it's the 24th January Popovic transcript, if my notes are correct. And if we could focus on line 17 and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a similar topic in relation to your reports that I'd now like to go through with you so, again, please bear with me reading into the record the prior testimony. And I begin: "Q. Mr. Butler, you are aware that you already said that a number of new documents have been obtained by the Office of the Prosecution. Would you agree with me that the documents obtained impact on every single aspect of your report because they were from the Drina Corps collection and it touches upon everything? Would you agree with that? "A. I would believe or I would concur that they are relevant. In many cases, they would not impact the report because they are -- in some cases, they are the identical documents or in other cases they are just larger collections of documents which serve to confirm an earlier analysis that I've conducted. So while every document is obviously important, whether it's relevant or whether it would change my conclusions is a case-by-case issue. That's it. "Q. You don't know that. "A. No, sir, I don't know the unknown. "Q. The new documents might infirm -- and might confirm but you don't know until you look at all the new documents along with your reports; is that correct? "A. Yes, sir. In the perfect world, I would have several years necessary to do that." First of all, sir, does this transcript section that I've just read accurately reflect the testimony that you gave as you remember giving it in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And would you maintain that same testimony if asked these same questions here today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My view is essentially the same. From the documents that I have had the opportunity to review, from the collections that were not available to me at the time, those documents tend to confirm the analysis and the conclusions that I draw in the reports. In many cases they are just exact copies of documents that I already have from another military unit, the report. And, again, I have seen nothing to date which causes me to pause and suggest that the narrative reports that I drafted in 2003 are no longer valid. I suggest one of the reasons why I'm here and why the prosecutor keeps offering me as a witness in this particular case is because of the fact that with the thousands or tens of thousands of documents that have found through the-- that the Office of the Prosecutor has found or obtained through the years, you know, the fact is that the narrative reports that I have drafted still reflect the logical layout of facts related to Srebrenica and the activities of the VRS in July of 1995. There has been no alternative narrative surfaced by anyone in those intervening years which suggest that my narrative view and the conclusions therein are not valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you say the documents that you've been able to review from these collections that were not available to you at the time, don't you really mean those documents that were in the bundle given to you by Mr. Peter McCloskey of the Prosecution as well as any that you may have reviewed on the EDS system? Isn't that a fair definition of the documents that you would have reviewed that were not available at the time you did your reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say simply Mr. McCloskey but other members of the Office of the Prosecutor would confront me with documents. Again, I would remind you that I did testify in the Karadzic case and it was a different trial team and therefore, again, other prosecutors from other cases providing me documents. And again, as I've noted, I've never had the impression that I've been denied access to any material that I felt that I needed to see or wanted to see that would be germane to my analysis or certainly my testimony here. But, you know, I concede that there are tens of thousands of documents that the OTP has obtained through the years which I have not been able to review and, again, I don't know the unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this. Apart from the documents that either Mr. McCloskey or some other Prosecution counsel selected for you to review, have you individually found documents on the EDS system out of your own searches that you've also reviewed that fall under this opinion or conclusion that you've just stated to us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if I can understand correctly, while you've had access to the EDS system, you have not actually utilised the EDS system to independently look for documents and you've only looked at those documents selected by the Prosecution for you to review?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, compound. There are several questions in there. It's hard to answer all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, would you rephrase, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's start at the beginning, sir. Is it correct that while you've had access to the EDS or electronic disclosure system, you have not actually utilised the EDS system to locate documents of your own accord?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be accurate probably for the last two years, perhaps even three years, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would it also be correct that when you say none of the documents that you looked at that were not available to you when you drafted your reports have caused you to reconsider the conclusions in your reports, are you referring to only documents that would have been selected and provided to you by Prosecution counsel from the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to call up 1D1261 in e-court. It will be page 2 of the e-court version which should correlate to transcript page 20352 of the 24 January Popovic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, this is in relation to section 4 of your report for the responsibilities of the VRS Brigade commander. And I'd like to have you follow along as I read from line 6 and then I'll have some questions about that: "Q. Now, when you reviewed the materials, so it would be my understanding that you read all this, all those laws which are written in a plain language, trying to understand what the disciplinary authority of a brigade commander is. "A. Yes, sir. I believe that was crucial with respect to understanding, you know, the authority limits as well as the potential league limits that a brigade commander or even a corps commander would be faced with, with respect to his role in ensuring the discipline of his subordinates. "Q. And did you try to make a parallel between your experience in the United States Army? "A. No, sir. That's why we have about a million lawyers to do that. "Q. And did you obtain any assistance from the lawyers within the OTP in drafting this part of your report? "A. No, sir. Like I said, my goal was not to find out what our lawyers were saying about it. My goal was to go out via the investigation and to find out what the appropriate VRS military prosecutors and military judges were saying about how these were applied. "Q. So would I be right in saying that in this section, section 4, it is in your capacity as a former soldier, your layman understanding of this most important topic? "A. Yes, sir. It is my understand of this topic, and if I'm defined as a layman, so be it." Does this selection of the transcript appear to accurately recite the testimony that you gave in the Popovic case as to these questions, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was a rather spirited exchange between myself and Mr. Stephane Bourgon. Clearly, Mr. Bourgon was taking advantage of the fact that as a former member of the OTP staff, he had a very inside view of the role of the military analysts, as having used them himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you'll forgive my reading -- my reading not being as spirited as the exchange may have been, but do I have to ask you, would you -- would your answers to these questions change or would you in essence repeat the same answers if I were to ask the questions at this trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only -- the change I would say is a technical one where it says "league," it should be "legal." But my answer would not change. Obviously, my goal in researching the VRS military prosecutor's office or the RS prosecutor's military offices at some point it went from the VRS to the Ministry of Defence control, was from a perspective of how they were applying it in the context of what was happening on the ground in 1995 during the conflict. It was not to get an opinion from any legal analyst from the Office of the Prosecutor or whether or not those were proper applications of the law or not proper applications of the law. My goal was just to explain what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you consider, as you sit there today, that this -- I believe it's section 4 of that particular report, can be relied upon in an expert sense by a Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe it is a fair accounting of the various mechanisms by which VRS military commanders had at their disposal at the time in order to enforce discipline among their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could for a moment turn to another transcript at 1D1260, page 37 in e-court which should be transcript page 20157 of the 22 January proceedings in the Popovic case. And if we could focus on line 12 and onwards, sir. And I propose to read for you again what may have been a spirited exchange, I don't know, but I think we can get through it faster if I just read it to you and ask for your comments upon it, if there are any, to indicate changes. So please, follow along from line 12, it begins: "Q. I want to talk a little bit about -- we discussed independence of you, were kind enough," pardon me, it's, "or you were kind enough to say you're human, as we all can see, and that you may have certain biases. Do you agree with me, sir, that you're not an independent outsider? "A. Yes, sir. "Q. And would you also agree with me that you're not independent per se? "A. That entirely depends on how you define per se. "Q. Okay. Well, let's look at your testimony in the Blagojevic case, pages 4755, lines 13 through 18, where you say, 'You are not independent per se.' Why don't you tell me, sir, what you mean by per se? "A. Okay. I'm not independent inasmuch as I work for the Office of the Prosecutor and, in that context, the material that I am reviewing for the most part is within the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor. I am independent in so much as the purpose, the focus and the conclusions of my analysis. "Q. Okay. We'll get to that shortly, I'm sure. And you also describe yourself, sir, as being an integrated member of the OTP; correct? "A. I believe it was an integrated member of the investigative team. If I said OTP, I certainly mean within the Srebrenica team. "Q. And you also describe yourself not only as being integrated but as a strategic member of the OTP, do you not? "A. With respect to the Srebrenica team and investigation, yes, sir." Now, does this have -- have we accurately seen everything -- seen how you recall testifying as to these specific questions, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've accurately recounted the testimony, I think is what you were saying, and yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is that all truthful? Is there any part that you think needs an additional clarification on your part?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I mean, as the -- you know, obviously within the broader context of the discussion, I am well aware, as Mr. Ostojic was pointing out, that there was certainly a perception of bias based on my association with the Srebrenica trial team and with the Office of the Prosecutor. It is obviously something I've dealt with through the years and has been a topic of discussion in previous cases. How much bias there is and whether it affects my work, obviously, is an issue that the Defence can raise and the Court will take into account when it reviews my work. With respect to the last issue, again, I was integrated into the Srebrenica team as their military analyst. The OTP is a big place and I would not suggest that somehow I was integrated into the OTP in the same manner. But as their military analyst, it was my job to be available as a resource to them. Consequently I had to be with them. I did not sit in their direct area but certainly I was engaged in discussions with their various individuals on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now in relation to the work that you did while at the OTP, would you agree with me that this type of work is what is commonly referred to or known especially in the intelligence community as more historical analysts' work insofar as in your reports you're not being asked or tasked to do any predictive analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe I have a definition of what that means and I'd like to go through it with you. If we can have page 56 of this same transcript, which should correlate to transcript page 20186 of the underlying transcript, and I'd like to start at line 20 -- whoops. If we can go ten pages forward, and then if we could focus on line 24. And again to make sure that the record is clear, this would then be the 66th page in e-court of this transcript whereas the underlying transcript page remains transcript page 20186. And, sir, again if you could bear with me, I believe this is part of your answer dealing with the description of what this all means: "A. ... however, as I've noted in the context of my very first report, it's not designed to be a historical overview. There are many political, there are many military, there are many diplomatic issues that are obviously related to these things that are beyond my ability to analyse and intelligently comment on. So in that respect, you know, I go back to the original purposes of my report, which were to set the framework for the military context and how they related to the crime bases that were being investigated with respect to the actual linkage of military units to crime scenes and the actual roles and responsibilities of individuals designated as commanders or other members of those units with respect to their roles and responsibilities under the VRS rules as they applied. By design, that is where I limited my analytical focus to." Sir, have I -- does this accurately reflect your testimony on this matter and do you still stand by, and are you satisfied with these answers as being correct and truthful?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is how I testified in response to this question. My answer has not changed in this respect. I lay out the objectives of my reports very clearly in the introductions of my reports, and what it is limited to. It has never been my intention to create a broad-based historical accounting of Srebrenica in July of 1995. One only has to go as far as the UN report and other various national reports to find that information. And again, with respect to the predictive part of the discussion, I was looking at and remain in this context looking at a static point in time, that the events that occurred in July of 1995. Obviously, as it is a historical event, nobody is asking me to take the events of what happened in July of 1995 and extrapolate how that might affect what the VRS will do months or years later. So, again, in that sense, it's a historical product. It's dealing with a static event in time. It is not taking that static event and then trying to predict future military behaviour based off of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And am I correct that the intentions and review of your analysis focused on, in addition to the limited military documents that the Office of the Prosecution had in its possession, also to the intercepts or alleged intercepts of radio communications by the ABiH which you also were tasked to integrate into your analysis and reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say limited military documents, because, you know, certainly 13.000 military documents is far more than I am normally accustomed to having at my disposal when asked to answer these types of questions. It also did, though, as you are correct, include an analysis of the ABiH intercepted radio communications and how that fell into the context of the military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in relation to this type of reporting that you did do, what we've agreed is the historical analysis reporting method, would you agree with me that in the US army, as an intelligence officer, such form of reporting was not your primary purpose although you did on occasion produce such products?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the sense that, again, my military customer's only interest in what happened historically is off of the basis of what that can then be used to allow them to predict future actions or events by an armed adversary and take advantage of them. So while I've obviously created various military reports in this narrative style throughout my career, the focus on those reports is less as to what happened at a particular point in time and far more on what that means projected into the future with respect to capabilities and intentions. So that's what I mean when this is not normally the type of work that I do. Obviously in my Srebrenica narrative reports there is no discussion of future capabilities or intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, roughly speaking, what percentage of your work that you normally did within the US army intelligence corps would have been this type of historical analysis as opposed to the more predictive issue type of reporting that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a percentage, but clearly the ability to understand the historical context, in any degree, is important to be able to accurately predict future intentions or capabilities. So unless it was a particularly technical report about a particular piece of communications equipment or something of that nature, the reality, if it was a broader military event that occurred on the ground or a broader political event that occurred, I mean, I would obviously have to discuss the historical context of that in order to be able to lay the foundation for a future assessment of potential courses of actions by an opponent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as part of the work that you did with the Office of the Prosecutor for the Srebrenica team of the Office of the Prosecutor, could you clarify for us if you sat in planning meetings where the Prosecution staff discussed and decided how to draft indictments against officers of the VRS in relation to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my time here, I did sit in planning meetings related to the indictments of both General Krstic and Colonel Blagojevic and Major Jokic. As noted, my role was again to be able to advise them as to, you know, the military documents and the contextual view that I understood of the military so they understood at least my perception of what the military situation was or was not occurring at the time for their -- for their purposes in writing the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, was it only the understanding or was it also a matter of advising them on what body of evidence would be available and therefore to make any technical assessment of how successful an indictment drafted in one way or another would be in view of the available evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, just as I did not operate in isolation, certainly neither did our lawyers. The lawyers on the various trial teams had a very good understanding of the body of the documents in question, as well as the body of the intercepts in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They knew exactly what the limits of those were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did you advise them on it as well, to say, well, this is a lot or there it's perhaps -- you should be cautious there because the body of evidence might not be abundant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I certainly with respect to advising them on a potential legal strategy -- it probably would shock you to learn that lawyers don't like taking advice about things like that from non-lawyers. So my role in that was technical, to advise them of what documents that we had, what my interpretation of the meaning of it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, many persons in this courtroom, being lawyers, can decide whether they are shocked or not. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to follow up on something you just said, your technical role, and again I understand that you previously testified, and you might have just mentioned -- I can't see it in the transcript. I understand that you did not have a vote in the drafting of the indictment. That's understood. But in terms of providing documents, were you called upon or did you volunteer of your own accord, what evidence or documentation could be utilised to successfully prosecute indictments once they were drafted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that that is slightly backwards because, again, in the sense of the original purpose of my reports, you know, as working aids for the Office of the Prosecutor and for the investigators, they already had access to my current understanding of what the military situation was or what the issues relating to command and control were or what my views of the role of the security branch, prior to them actually writing an indictment. So it wasn't a situation where I was trying to conform my view or get them to conform their indictment to my views. I mean, they knew my opinions and views going in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you've mentioned the three cases that were -- that proceeded to trial during the time period that you were at the Office of the Prosecutor. Did you have any role at any time while at the Office of the Prosecutor in relation to either suggesting amendments to or selecting evidence for the Mladic case or the Mladic indictment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never suggested amendments for the Mladic indictment. And in fact, I don't think I can even -- I don't believe I've even read the current indictment of General Mladic in its entirety. So in that particular context, yeah, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I would move on to another topic. I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, I believe there was two trials during his time frame, not three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there were two trials but I think that three accused were named.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Three accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise if I misspoke in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that you had some assistance that worked with you in the drafting of your reports. In relation to those individuals, could you tell me whether they too had military and indeed military analyst experience and whether they had any prior previous academic or military experience in relation to the JNA, the VRS, the All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The people who were working directly with me, one of them was a former, although she had military service, she was a -- by trade or profession, she was a police criminal analyst, and the other person working with me was an administrative assistant, I don't recall she had any military experience whatsoever. And, you know, the members of the -- or the group of individuals that we had doing sorting and translation of military documents, again, they were there for translation and language support. They were not people I was going to lean on for military advice or expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Focusing on the persons that worked directly with you or assisted you directly in your work, have any of them authored any professional publications on any of the topics that you collaborated with them on or that they assisted you with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get a foundation of what kind of assistance? I mean there is many, many ways to assist, and so far we don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness has just stated what type of assistance he has. I'm referring to those assistants. He hasn't identified them by name but he has identified them by education. I'm sure that Mr. Butler has in his mind precisely who his assistants were that he's just now described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My objection is we heard there is people helping him with translation, we hear that there is other assistants but we have not heard what they are assisting him with, aside from his report in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's limit it to the members of the team. Is that, Mr. Ivetic, what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware, and again, the relevance escapes me at this moment, Mr. Ivetic, but nevertheless let's first get the question on the table, have any of the members of the team in which you worked authored any professional publications on any of the topics that you collaborated with them on, or that they assisted you with? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the two individuals that I have in mind, Ms. Amanda Brettle and Ms. Sally Latin, have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to yourself, sir, I believe apart from the one book authored in 2004 or co-authored with first Lieutenant Epstein of the USMC in 2004 you have not published any published works on the same topics as contained in the reports that you authored for purposes of trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a book. It was an article in a military law review magazine and the topic of that was not related to Srebrenica 1995. It was a broader legal issue on the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and its potential relevance to US military Tribunals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to move through some of your reports, to highlight certain preliminary methodological issues. If we could first start off with your report on the responsibilities of the Main Staff which is 65 ter number 05601, and if we can pull up that report, and while we wait for that, sir, perhaps a general question: What type of reasoning methodology did you use in preparing this report? Would it be described as being deductive reasoning or inductive reasoning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of the conclusions would be related to deductive reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have some help on what Mr. Ivetic means by that? Because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, rather than testifying I'm going to ask Mr. Butler what he means by it since he apparently does understand what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Deductive reasoning, as I understand it from an analytical tool perspective, is taking some facts and using then using those to draw a conclusion. At the moment, I don't -- I know intuitively what inductive reasoning is but at the moment I couldn't give you a technical definition of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But in any event you consider your report to have been the deductive form of reasoning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean I am working off of issues that I consider to be obviously known facts and, you know, deducing conclusions as to what they mean based on those facts and how they line up in a logical sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, apparently the witness does not fully understand your question because he has difficulties in defining what inductive reasoning is, so could you please explain to the witness what you meant by that so that the witness can also understand whether the one system excludes the other or if he says in -- many conclusions are obtained by deductive reasoning, that whether the others perhaps were then obtained by inductive reasoning. So would you please put to the witness what you understand by inductive reasoning so that he can fully answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My understanding, and again this was suggested to me by our expert consultant, but it's whether it's a process whereby you begin with the thesis and then build upon it or whether you review materials and then conclude a thesis at the end, so it's whether it's an ends-based approach or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that -- more clear to you, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fairly consistent. I mean, where I -- where I take both deductive and inductive reasoning in this is the fact that I recognise that as a component of my work, I am somewhat bound by the existing indictments in a various case. So I don't have a complete free range to explore any particular issue that I want because those issues would not be relevant to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can have a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will take the break but not until after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at half past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness will be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile I use the opportunity for the following matter: During Witness Emir Turkusic's testimony on the 30th of August, the Prosecution used the stabiliser fin from a 12- millimetre mortar which was allegedly recovered at the scene of the Markale II shelling. Its pictures have been admitted as Exhibits P2053 as shown on transcript page 15924. The artifact itself was not admitted awaiting further clarification on whether it can be admitted in the present case despite the fact that it had already been admitted in the Karadzic case. Having consulted with the Registry, the Chamber understands that the same piece of physical evidence can be admitted in two different cases, considering that it is kept in the Registry vault. A photo of the exhibit and a surrogate sheet indicating that the original is kept in the vault are included in e-court with a note that it is also admitted in another case. The Chamber notes that if the exhibit would need to be examined, the regular chain of custody procedure would need to be followed, and any forensic analysis of the physical evidence required would need to be done in consultation with the Karadzic Trial Chamber. Considering the above, the Chamber hereby admits the stabiliser fin into evidence as Exhibit P2053, together with the pictures already admitted into evidence and the Chamber instructs the Prosecution to upload a surrogate sheet and the Chamber instructs the Registry to add the surrogate sheet to Exhibit 2053 once it has been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready, you may proceed. Mr. Butler, we had to deal with a small procedural item. Apologies for having you wait. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at the document that we have up on e-court, sir, this is again your report from 2006 on the VRS Main Staff and it is reflected therein that this particular report was mandated because of the context of the prosecutor versus Miletic et al trial, and due to the Prosecution having obtained a large documentary collection commonly referred to as the -- and it's said in there, "Drina Corps archives." Now, these Drina Corps archives that you've identified, am I correct that they are not the official archives of the Drina Corps but, rather, are the conglomeration of documents from several sources commonly referred to the other day by Mr. McCloskey and I as the quote/unquote Drina Corps collection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's consistent with my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you personally participate in any efforts to track down or obtain this so-called Drina Corps collection from the various sources from whence it was gathered?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly participated in efforts by the trial team or the Srebrenica team to find military documents. Of course, these would be included in that during my tenure here employed. I was not involved obviously after I left the Tribunal in November of 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that you end up utilising quite a few documents from this Drina Corps collection for purposes of this report that we have on the screen, which is 65 ter number 05601, and also in your Srebrenica narrative report as revised, and in your oral testimony these previous days before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I used the documents from the Drina Corps collection broadly. We had other documents that were coming in from -- from different sources and I used those in my revised narrative. I did use the Drina Corps collection documents in my 2006 report. And the tactic that the prosecutor has used in respect with me on that is in order to discuss those documents, obviously I've been made aware of them and I've discussed those documents in my testimony from Popovic and other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to focus on this 2006 report that we have up on the screen. For purposes of this report, I think based upon the testimony that you've given today in relation to other questions of mine, that the documents you would have used from that collection for purposes of generating this 2006 report, those would have been the ones that were selected and provided to you by Prosecution counsel, is that -- is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean I had a list of -- I had one individual from the Office of the Prosecutor, my former assistant, would at various points in time as they were exploiting the Drina Corps collection and cataloguing it, she would send me the various lists of documents from the index that they were developing. So because I had that basic document list, I had to a very large degree an ability to pick the documents I wanted to use, to explore certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I understand. Now, prior to utilising the documents from this Drina Corps collection, did you personally undertake to either take steps yourself or ask that steps be taken to confirm the provenance and authenticity of those documents from the collection that came from various sources?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm aware of the protocols that the Office of the Prosecutor takes in order to verify the authenticity of a document. My -- obviously my practice is that if I'm not convinced that the document is authentic I don't use it in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So were you relying upon the protocols and relying upon other people to do their work or did you affirmatively undertake steps either yourself or to direct others to check the provenance of those documents that ultimately you did use in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I relied on the individuals within the Office of the Prosecutor for -- with, you know, verifying the authenticity of the document, that it was not -- and when I talk about authenticity I'm obviously referring to a document not being a forgery. Because I'm aware of the background of how they normally do that, and how the investigative process works to do that, I have a high degree of confidence in it. I have to confess I'm not exactly sure what you mean by provenance of a certain document, if you could explain that, I can, if necessary, comments on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. Provenance, where it came from, the source.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that for me would be the -- that would be part of the authentication process.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you undertake to investigate the chain of custody of these documents at any point in the process or to direct others to investigate the chain of custody of where these documents were held before arriving to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally investigate the chain of custody. I am aware of the various iterations that these documents went through prior to arriving to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you keep a log or list of what documents you utilised originated solely from the so-called Drina Corps collection as opposed to those that could be found in other sources that you had access to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, just like in my other reports, I cite the documents that I rely on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 3 of the English and 3 of the Serbian of this document, I'd like to focus on what you say there. It's in the middle of the -- of this last paragraph of your introduction to the report. And it says, "In their totality," well, first of all, here you're talking about how this particular report on the VRS Main Staff must be read in conjunction with your corps and brigade reports as well as the Srebrenica Military Narrative report, and then you say that: "In their totality, these reports form the foundation of my understanding of VRS military command and the specific linkage to the crimes as charged in the indictment. Also, utilising the same methodology as noted in these earlier works, I continue to rely primarily on a document-based analytical approach." Now, the question I have for you, sir, is you say primarily. Could you please identify for us what, if any, other analytical approaches comprised your methodology for this particular report, if any?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, as I've testified, I think it's last week now, clearly if I were producing a similar type of report for my normal customer, I would include in that report information related from human sources or HUMINT. As I also noted, I mean, obviously I am aware, as a member of the Prosecution team and with law enforcement in general, that these -- many of these same people would be testifying before the Court, and therefore it's the Court's responsibility to weigh their testimony and the information they provide on a variety of factors. As I've said, if there is anything artificial about these four reports per se it is because I rely almost totally on my analysis of documents and I only use witness testimony or human intelligence, as it were, in order to set the necessary limited context in order to make the rest of the report have any meaning. And I gave -- I guess I gave you that example of, you know, it doesn't make context of what's happening in a crime scene if you don't at least have somebody explain what the basis of the crime scene is occurring, you don't -- you can't lash up the military or other documents to it without at least that kind of basic knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could take a step backwards and look at the prior page in both versions of this report, which would be page 2, at the top of the page, it is recorded that the Drina Corps archives, which we now know to be the Drina Corps collection, are said to compose the bulk of the wartime records of the VRS Drina Corps and its subordinate units. Now, I take from this, sir, that you are relying upon someone else's representations as to the Drina Corps archives which we now know to be the Drina Corps collection. Could you please identify for us on whose representations are you relying for purposes of this statement in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be various lawyers and analysts, military analysts from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct in understanding this to imply that the Drina Corps collection may be the sole source for most of the actual VRS documents in the possession of the OTP that relate to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't draw that conclusion. There are a variety of documents that -- and document collections that I've encountered through the years that relate to the Drina Corps, and, again, I'm not necessarily saying you're wrong but I've never done a percentage analysis of what you're asking, so I can't intelligently comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair, sir. Now, if we look towards the middle of this same page in both languages, it is the second -- the second paragraph in the English, and it says there: "With respect to the second issue, a review of my earlier analytical products does indicate a necessity to expand on a number of issues directly related to the VRS Main Staff, particularly with respect to the positions and functions of the assistant commander for morale, legal and religious affairs; the chief of operations; and to a lesser extent the chief of security." Can we conclude or infer from this, sir, that your methodology of preparing this report did not focus on the commander of the Main Staff or the Chief of Staff, who was also the deputy commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree, because I believe that it's not possible to be able to understand the roles of the various principal staff officers, the assistant commander of morale, legal affairs or the chief of operations, or the assistant commander for intelligence and security, without having the ability to describe and discuss the roles of the commander and his Chief of Staff. I believe that is inherent in not only this particular report but the other command responsibility reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this: In the course of your review of documents, I take it that you had occasion to review a number of documents that were drafted by General Mladic, including those for which you only had the receiving end of that document, without any signature; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it the electronic versions of those, yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any indication of the quantity of such documents that you would have had access to and reviewed that were said to have originated from General Mladic, what quantity were signed by his own hand as opposed to sent out in his name, including those mysterious documents with the notation, "svojerucno," by his own hand that we saw that date from the time period when he was not physically present in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you asked me that question a couple of hours ago and my answer was that I've never done an analysis to determine which documents, you know, the percentage of documents that were signed personally by General Mladic versus those that are in possession of the OTP that are telegraph versions of them and I have not done an analysis to determine how many of the documents are signed by General Mladic and how many percentage of those documents have the ubiquitous SR on them. So I mean, I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, in relation to all those documents that say that they are signed or came from General Mladic, including those mysterious ones that say SR at the end, I would ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to the term "mysterious" as unnecessary, and I don't want the record to reflect that Mr. Butler agrees with that or has to argue with him about it. I don't think there is anything mysterious about them but that's for argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll be happy to call them ubiquitous like Mr. Butler did, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first listen what your question will be because the introduction -- let's forget about the introduction for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to focus on whatever portion of those documents that you looked at that originated from General Mladic that would have constituted the form of a military order to subordinate units and would ask you if I'm correct that not a single such document called upon subordinate units to commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to July 1995, and the scope of my analysis related to Srebrenica, I have not come across a document by General Mladic specifically ordering the execution of the prisoners. I would suggest that the order from General Mladic to Trbic with respect to the fuel for the reburial operation could arguably fall into that order directing the commission of a crime but, again, that's an issue beyond my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And beyond that one document, you don't recall any others that would even come close to fitting the definition of ordering a crime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A document signed by him with respect to Srebrenica, July 1995, I believe that is fair. I have -- I don't recall ever seeing a document like that. I obviously am not in a position to comment about other aspects and time periods as charged in the indictment, so --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And thank you for making that clarification. Whenever I ask you questions I'm asking specifically about the time period that you're talking about, which is July 1995, and Srebrenica. Now, in the course of your reports, all of them, and in the course of your narratives, both of them, both the original and the revised, and also in the testimony of prior cases that I've read, you do not mention very frequently or at all the Chief of Staff, the deputy commander of the VRS Main Staff, General Manojlo Milovanovic. Is that a conscious omission on your part of that individual?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conscious only in the sense that to the best of my knowledge and as reflected by the documents, his role in what I was looking at in my reports was limited. For example, again, I know that both the investigation and in his own commentary, he was not present in the Eastern Bosnian area, nor was he present exercising a command function at the VRS Main Staff headquarters. He was in fact dealing with issues pertaining to the western Krajina. So because of that, and because essentially for whatever purposes the VRS felt they needed to do, the logical chain of command did not go from General Mladic to General Milovanovic. It went in fact from General Mladic to General Miletic. As the chief of operations he was the person who would stand in for the Chief of Staff in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to link this with prior testimony you've given us, the General Milovanovic we have been talking about is the same individual whom you'll recall having had the discussion with in the presence of an interpreter, and I believe you said Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez, but first of all is that the same General Milovanovic we are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Could you perhaps be mistaken about the identity of Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez and perhaps was it Mr. Barry Hogan, who was present for that discussion that you recall? Would you permit that possibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean, it was many years ago and, again, it's not a topic that I have been asked very much so I certainly hold open the possibility that the investigator was not who I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to move again to some questions in relation to your Srebrenica narratives, and for the record, when I use the term "Srebrenica narrative," I'm referring to 65 ter numbers 04626, which is the original done for the Krstic case, and 04627, which is the 2002 revision of the same. Now, during the direct examination last week, and indeed even today, you have made reference to the fact and stressed several times that you wanted to stay away from witness references in your reports. In that regard, would you agree with me that your revised 2002 Srebrenica Military Narrative contains no fewer than 74 references to witness testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree or disagree. I've never actually gone through my own report to count how many times I might have cited a particular witness. My goal is to, again, use only the witness testimony for a very limited purpose. If it took 74 references to do that, again, I wouldn't -- wouldn't dispute that but, again, it's not my goal that I would -- that I'm asking the Court to rely on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this -- these references, whether it's 74, 75, for purposes of this question it doesn't matter. Am I correct that these references to witness testimony, all of them in the -- in the 2002 narrative relate to testimony that these witnesses gave in the first Srebrenica trial against General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In my initial narrative report I referenced them from witness statements. For ease of handling by the Court in going back and looking at these in the future environment, I used -- I based them off of their identifications and their testimony as offered during the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you undertake for purposes of this trial against General Mladic, to review and check if in fact these same witnesses even testified, let alone testified in the same manner as they had in Krstic, upon which you relied in your reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. As I believe I testified last week, I've not followed the events or testimony in this trial at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think we can agree, then, that since your 2002 report, using these witness testimonies, was authored, there have been at least, I think, five trials on Srebrenica before this Tribunal that you have, I believe, also appeared as a witness in, several before the state court in Sarajevo, if I could take you back to your time period when you were doing this type of work for US army intelligence, would such a report pass muster and be considered reliable if it had remained dated and referred to witness testimony that predated 2002 and ignored or did not deal with, I should say, any of the subsequent testimony of these or other witnesses that had come to light in the subsequent proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's a long, convoluted, many questions involved in one, and I doubt Mr. Butler would have written anything like that to the United States Army with witness testimony in it, so if he could break it down ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, did you want to ask as a matter of fact whether the lapse of time and the new developments since then, whether that would have created a risk of the report being outdated?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think he's answered that question. What I really want to ask is what would be the standard operating procedure in the US army for a report that would be so dated where there was indications that there were subsequent interviews or subsequent testimony by the same people. Would the standard procedure be to rely upon that report or to ask for an updated report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a relevant question? What the US army would do with that? Perhaps it's argumentative in the sense that you are telling this Court that you shouldn't use it. Is that what you want to convey as a message? Then we have understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, whether I want to convey it as a message, Your Honours, this witness has testified that based upon his experience and training as an operative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. Put a question as you wish and I think the matter is clear that you want certainly to draw our and the witness's attention to the fact that it was not updated since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may ask one follow-up question, then, whose decision was it not to update the report? Was it yours or was it by Prosecution counsel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never been asked by Prosecution counsel to update the narrative report, primarily because the Prosecution is well aware that under my current job responsibilities, there is no way that I could dedicate the time and the resources necessary to update it in the manner that -- that I would with want to and be satisfied that it was updated. I just do not have that time ability to do that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that but do you suppose another military analyst, another military expert, could pick up your work and run with it, as it were, to update it, check with new material and create a second report, either saying there are drastic differences or there aren't drastic differences? Would you expect that that could be done?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, a broader sense, I've been waiting now for 15 years for somebody to pick up all of the collective historical work related to this and run with it. Sadly, that has not been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might ask Mr. Lukic, if another military analyst does that whose report would it then be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me, Your Honours, instead of Mr. Lukic, it would be then the second military analyst obviously who I would expect generate a second report and then we would have the original report, the report of the second analyst, and then we would have a fuller picture of how much reliance we could place upon the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would no longer be his report. And my apologies to you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, it would no longer be his report. If I may just briefly consult, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, low volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, to take a bit of advantage because I know Mr. Stojanovic is on this issue, we were talking about having Marija Karall, perhaps if you would approve, start tomorrow morning because as you know from Mr. Groome she is leaving and we have spoken to Mr. Stojanovic and that appears to be okay, as far as we know with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So not Friday but tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I do understand that there is no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I discussed it with my colleague, Mr. Ivetic, and we decided that we could indeed start with that witness tomorrow morning, in the hope that Mr. Butler doesn't have anything against it, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue this matter, Mr. Butler, there is a request by the Prosecution to hear another witness starting tomorrow morning first, which may delay the conclusion of your testimony. Would that bother you or would you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm here at the convenience of the Court on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, as you know it's one hour time estimate so Mr. Butler knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour is 3600 seconds, as you know. Therefore, the Chamber has no objection that the continuation of the cross-examination of Mr. Butler will start after the testimony of the next witness to be called then tomorrow morning. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I forget what day it was but during the direct examination, you were shown a map that was said to be signed by General Mladic pertaining to the Krivaja operation, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you also confirm for me, sir, that the signature on that map, according to the results of your investigation, was placed on there at the earliest on the 13th of July, after the operation had already been completed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two signatures on that map which purport to be General Mladic's. I would suggest and my point of view is that the one that is in the middle of the map, which talks about Srebrenica being Serbian before, would fall into the category you suggested. He could have signed it on either the evening of the 12th or on the 13th. The signature that I am talking about is the one on the upper left-hand corner of the map which was part of the map when it was the graphic representation of the Srebrenica operations plan that the Drina Corps was briefing to the Main Staff. That particular signature, under the command and staff processes that the VRS followed, it would have been normal for the commander, General Mladic, to sign that prior to the initiation of the operation. He would not have signed that particular block on the upper left-hand corner on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is your answer based upon you understanding of what the practice would have been, or is it an affirmation that the investigation facts of your investigation have borne that to have been the case in reality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my understanding, based on the practice of the VRS. I'm not aware -- I'm not -- again, I wasn't at that particular meeting and I'm not aware. You know, there may have been witness testimony that discusses that but I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could just briefly get back to the Srebrenica trial narrative which is where we began this line of questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is supposed not to speak aloud, to whisper is okay, otherwise you consult after the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may, sir, in the Srebrenica trial narrative, and first of all, I'd like to focus on Kravica and the incidents there. In your discussion of the incidents at Kravica, I have never seen in any of the narratives or in the testimonies that you've given, any acknowledgement or reference of any fire-fight at that location between guards and detainees who had taken over a weapon and in which one policeman was killed and one wounded and perhaps another passerby wounded. Did you have knowledge of such an incident having taken place at the Kravica location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I wrote my narratives, the documents that we had were the documents that we had. I have become aware, though, in the intervening years, that that is an issue that had come up and that various parties on the VRS and the Republika Srpska police side had raised the prospect that the people who were killed in Kravica were a direct result of an attempt by individual Muslim prisoners to potentially escape. I believe I've addressed that issue and why I don't believe that that overall is the case in the Karadzic trial. He asked me that specific question and I gave a rather lengthy answer as to why I did not believe that that was the case, primarily based on the outcomes of all of the individuals who were at the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, talking about long answers, I'm looking at the clock, quarter past 2. It's a matter to be explored perhaps in further detail tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After the intervening witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, especially since the witness threatened us with long answers. We will adjourn for the day. Mr. Butler, I again instruct you not to speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, either given or still to be given. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would like to see you back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not tomorrow morning but because we'll first hear the testimony of another witness, but could I ask you an assessment when would Mr. Butler have to remain stand-by for later tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told that the witness could be accomplished in approximately one hour so I would imagine by the time of the second session we would be ready to resume with Mr. Butler.
